articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Electrically Small Antennas' (Digest No.136)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: The author gives a brief definition of an electrically small antenna. The characteristic expected of an electrically-short antenna is low radiation resistance and large reactance hence very small instantaneous bandwidth with respect to the impedance of normal radio equipment. The author considers four antennas: the short dipole (or monopole), transmission line antenna, short notch antenna, and the small loop antenna. The features and applications of each antenna are discussed. The matching problems of small antennas is also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: Crossed-field-antennas (CFAs) are novel antenna systems which are structurally small (can be typically < lambda /100 in size), wide bandwidth and efficient radiators. Constructed prototypes which are also good receivers, have been successful in the MF, HF and VHF ranges. Basically, the CFA stimulates E and H fields to be in precise time-synchronism close to the antenna structure and hence provides a source of intense power radiation from a small compact volume. Since time-synchronism is controlled outwith or independently from the antenna structure, then the requirement of a specific antenna structure size to achieve radiated power is not a critical feature and hence small size CFAs can be constructed. The authors discuss the phasing unit and impedance matching, input impedance and bandwidth, the effect of phase change between the E and H fields, and working voltages.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Medium frequency body loop antenna for use underground
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: Radio communication underground in mines is possible by a variety of propagation mechanisms. Where there is a need for the communication system to be independent of special-purpose cables, such as 'leaky feeders', then maximum propagation range is only possible if low-frequency radio systems are used. The usual requirement that the equipment be portable imposes severe restrictions on the antenna. The author reviews this problem briefly and describes a loop antenna, developed specifically for this application, which is worn by the operator. The magnetic dipole or small loop has particular advantages over the more conventional short electric antenna when both are surrounded by a lossy dielectric medium. The need to achieve maximum magnetic moment is discussed as is its relationship to the loop geometry and the required operating bandwidth. The effect of the operator's body on the antenna's characteristics is also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On the resonant frequency of the normal mode helical antenna excited by a loop
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: The resonant performance of the electrically small helical antenna excited by a loop is investigated by the moment method, using second order B-spline functions as basis functions. Although the antennas studied are electrically very small, the program provides convergent results which agree well with those of the experiment. It is shown that the resonant frequency of the antenna is closely related to the helix parameters. When the wire length is held constant, the resonant frequency increases with the pitch and decreases when the radius of the helix is increased. With a fixed helix diameter, a critical turn spacing exists which determines whether the resonant length is greater or less than one half wavelength. By adjusting the turn spacing of the helix, a specific resonant frequency can be obtained.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Thick film printed high-T/sub c/ superconducting small loop antenna
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: A thick film printed high-T/sub c/ superconducting small loop antenna of YBCO is fabricated on an alumina substrate and experimental results are presented at 440 MHz together with those of an identical silver antenna. The example printed YBCO loop antenna system shows just a marginal improvement on the silver system at 77 K. However, the YBCO material provided has a low cross-over frequency with copper at 77 K due to problems with contanation of the YBCO with the alumina substrate. If the YBCO thick film material had better surface resistance, the superconducting antenna would have had a much better performance in power gain.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: System considerations of a superconducting loop antenna
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: With reference to the design of an electrically small loop antenna using superconducting components, the authors attempt to answer the following questions: can the matching unit be made smaller because it is many times bigger than the antenna in some examples? High efficiency is often of secondary importance to bandwidth and noise constraints, what will be the dimensions and the electromagnetic properties of the cryogenic apparatus? How do the system requirements constrain the superconductivity specification? In some systems will partial deployment of superconducting components be advantageous? Some ongoing practical work on planar superconducting components is mentioned to illustrate specific points.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A controlled electrically small antenna for the evaluation of radiated emission testing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: The use of screened rooms for spurious radiated emission measurements has been common practice for many years. At low frequencies the rooms cannot be made anechoic due to the depth of radio absorbent material (RAM) required, and the measurements are affected by cavity and other resonances associated with the propagation mechanisms operating in the room. Measurement uncertainties of +or-30 dB or more have been observed. The authors are involved in a study of the feasibility of reducing these measurement errors to an acceptable level. In order to carry out the study, an electromagnetically representative device-under-test (DUT) has been developed. The authors describe the design philosophy of the DUT. They also present some preliminary results of experiments carried out to investigate the effects the position of the DUT inside the screened room has on its operation with reference to its operation on an open field test site.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Some HP system design considerations for aircraft
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: The author discusses the fundamental limitations of electrically small radiators and their significance to electrically small antennas. Some of the parameters are derived. Systems incorporating electrically small radiators are constrained by fundamental limitations to be either inefficient or narrowband. These conditions are apparent in the case of aircraft HF (2-30 MHz) antenna systems, particularly for small aircraft at the low end of the band. The author discusses the HF antenna problems for aircraft, in particular the need to distinguish between the airframe and the antenna. The types of antenna used, loops and notches, are discussed. Examples of measurements for a BAC 1-11 airliner and a helicopter are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new approach to the design of a broadband active loop antenna 50 kHz-30 MHz
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrically Small Antennas
abstract: The author discusses improvements in the design of active loop receiving antennas. The improvements include segmenting a large diameter single loop into a number of equal smaller loops. This allows the source inductance to be adjusted as required. When this loop array is connected to a common base amplifier a substantial improvement in sensitivity is achieved in the frequency range 3 to 30 MHz. Loop antennas have other attributes. Directivity in the horizontal plane aids rejection of unwanted signals and the absence of a null in the vertical plane makes high angle skywave reception much better than with the vertical monopole. The loop antenna can also be effectively decoupled from local sources of interference which is not possible with monopole antennas and which have the added disadvantage that the feeder forms part of the antenna.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
